fatal_errors: The proposed composition modification does not reconstruct the governing intervention of high-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering.
The hypothesis excludes multiphase alloys, whereas the target behavior occurs in an approximately 83% FCC/17% BCC nanocrystalline microstructure.

Changing composition simultaneously changes atomic-size mismatch, chemical ordering, phase stability, elastic constants, and stacking-fault energy, so the experiment cannot uniquely attribute strengthening to lattice distortion or short-range order.
XRD peak broadening is not a unique measure of lattice distortion because crystallite size, microstrain, defects, and instrumental broadening also contribute.
No external or cited evidence supports the asserted primary role of short-range order or the predicted 10–30% increase.
explanation: The response is a coherent and falsifiable alternative hypothesis for strengthening in single-phase high-entropy alloys. It provides a baseline, boundaries, mechanical tests, structural measurements, and an explicit falsification rule. However, it does not recover the target processing route, process window, nanocrystalline FCC/BCC structure, or dominant synergy among Hall–Petch strengthening, milling-induced dislocation density, and solid-solution strengthening. It also misses the target quantitative outcomes of about 675 Hv hardness, 1894 MPa compressive strength, and 1238 MPa yield stress, as well as the cast-alloy baseline and intergranular fracture behavior. Its causal discrimination is limited because composition is used to alter both lattice mismatch and short-range order at once, while potentially introducing several other strengthening and phase-stability changes.
